commit message:
use the same gauss filter for deconv methods

In deconvf the gauss filter is defined as exp(-0.5*(f/f1)**2),
the default is f1=0.5 corresponding to a cut-off frequency in Hz.
In deconv_iter it is defined as exp(-0.25*(2*pi*f/f0)**2) without the dt term,
the default width is f0=3.

The relation between f1 and f0 is f1=f0/(2**0.5 * pi),
so the default in deconv_iter of f0=3 corresponds to f1=0.67
(being the cut-off frequency of the low-pass filter).

I now switched to the same definition as in deconvf and also use the same default value 0.5.

commit message:
fix invalid length error with meshio.CellBlock

In commit [60d11b70] of meshio the length of `CellBlock`, a subclass of
`namedtuple`, is redefined to the length of the `data` attribute. This breaks
`namedtuple._replace`, where the length of the newly created `CellBlock` is
verified. This patch circumvents the problem by using the `CellBlock`
constructor directly instead of `namedtuple._replace`.

[60d11b70]: https://github.com/nschloe/meshio/commit/60d11b705c9b9074284feefdb7475db0410953e9

commit message:
support numpy.number array bases in lru_cache

`types.lru_cache` uncovers the bases of `numpy.ndarray` arguments and stores
weak references to the bases with a clean-up function. If the base is a
`numpy.number`, then it is impossible to get a weak reference and `lru_cache`
raises. This patch fixes the problem by holding a weak reference to the array
that references the base if the base is a `numpy.number`.

The above situation occurs when calling `numpy.ndarray` with a `numpy.number`
as base, which is used in `evaluable.InsertAxis.evalf`.

author: Gertjan van Zwieten <gertjanvanzwieten@evalf.nl>
commit message:
allow numpy 1.24 (#770)

Revert #759 and fix unit tests.

PR #759 excluded the latest Numpy version (1.24) because of failing unit
tests check:sqrt and check:log2-complex in Github actions due to lack of
accuracy. Confusingly, tests never failed locally, and only randomly on
Github - rerunning a failed job would occasionally result in success. Out
of caution, the version was excluded until the cause of this situation was
known.

The problem is now understood to be caused by vectorized routines that
make use of the AVX-512 CPU extensions. None of the local machines used
in testing supported these instructions, and only some of Github's
randomly assigned machines do which explains the
random failures. CPU capabilities can be queried using Numpy's new
`show_runtime` method, and absence of extensions AVX512F, AVX512CD and
AVX512_SKX correlates 100% with passing tests and vice versa.
The problem in sqrt is caused by the fact the `evaluable.Sqrt` evaluates
using `numpy.power`, but compares the result with `numpy.sqrt`, and the
vectorized routines result in slightly different results causing the
test to miss its tolerance threshold. The log2 test, likewise, is
evaluated differently than its reference. This PR fixes the tolerance
issue by setting the reference result equal to the way the operation is
evaluated, so that the tolerance is always reached regardless of CPU.

What remains unclear is why this problem arose with the release of Numpy
1.24, as the AVX-512 code paths were merged prior to version 1.22. Several
AVX-512 related commits have followed since, but it is not clear which
caused the particular differences that caused these tests to fail. Once
we have local access to a machine that supports AVX-512 extensions we
can bisect Numpy to find the culprit and perhaps understand the true
source of the numerical change (however slight), but in the meantime we
can conclude that there is no reason to maintain the ban on Numpy 1.24.

commit message:
add parallel.Manager, subset of multiproc.Manager

With `parallel.fork` data cannot be shared between processes using shared
memory, except for arrays. `multiprocessing.Manager` supports sharing data via
pipes or sockets using pickle as serialization. This patch adds a minimal subset of
`multiprocessing.Manager` to `parallel`, supporting shared lists and dicts. If
parallel mode is disabled, a fake manager is returned which creates regular
lists and dicts, eliminating overhead of serialization, transfering and
deserialization.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
prevent parsing func calls as old-style operators

The old-style operators `d`, `n` and `J` - not to be confused with the
functions with the same name, included by default in the namespace - are
identified as such during tokenization. The tokenizer incorrectly matches an
operator when followed by a left parenthesis symbol. As a consequence it is
impossible to parse a function-style operator under certain conditions. For
example `d:i(u, x_i)_j` is currently tokenized as `jacobian of i, '(', ...`
instead of `variable 'd', consumes 'i', '(', ...`. This patch fixes the problem
by adding a look-ahead test for left parentheses after a potential match of an
old-style operator.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
add types.hashable_function

Plain functions are not Nutils hashable, because there is no reliable
information to generate a hash from: the name of the function cannot be used
because the behavior might be non-deterministic or can simply be changed
between different runs, and the bytecode only describes a single function, not
the functions that are being called or variables that are being accessed from
outer scopes, if any. I hear you say: 'but the dependent functions can be
distilled from the bytecode,' and: 'the closure variables are stored in the
function object.' Well, I wish you good luck with implementing a solid hash in
a Tuesday evening. This leaves us with the possibility to explicitly add a
Nutils hash to functions that need one. This commit introduces the decorator
`types.hashable_function` for this purpose.

Github Actions we cannot find the location of the library directory where MKL

commit message:
use affine root coords as geom if possible

Before 5034398d3 the geometry of a rectilinear mesh with uniform vertices was
an affine transformation of the root coordinates. In patch 5034398d3 this
special case was removed due to a pending change in the transform chains for
structured topologies: the replacement of the transformation that places an
element in the root space with an index, thereby giving every element unit
square root coordinates.

The effect of this change is a suboptimal gradient of the geometry to the root
coordinates. Since the geometry is now always the inner product of a linear
basis with vertices, the gradient of the geometry does not simplify to a
constant if the vertices are evenly spaced.

This patch restores the special cased geometry for rectilinear meshes defined
by numbers of elements by creating a reference geometry out of the (unit
square) root coordinates and the element index.

commit message:
Reduce _intbounds evaluations

This patch changes the logic in Array._intbounds with the aim to reduce
the number of potentially expensive array evaluations.

Formerly, evaluation always happened for scalar constant arrays. The
_intbounds_impl method was called only for non-scalar or non-constant
arrays.

The new implementation always calls _intbounds_impl, which evaluates
constant scalar arrays in its default implementation. The result is that
evaluation is avoided for all arrays that provide their own
_intbounds_impl.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
Evaluable to Python code compiler (#859)

Previously `Evaluable`s were evaluated by looping over all dependencies and
calling `Evaluable.evalf`. For `1 + 2 + 3` (not simplified) this boils down to

```python
serialized = [
    [Constant(1).evalf],
    [Constant(2).evalf],
    [Constant(3).evalf],
    [Add.evalf, 0, 1],
    [Add.evalf, 3, 2],
]
def eval():
    values = []
    for op, *args in serialized:
        values.append(op(*map(values.get, args)))
    return values[-1]
```

This PR replaces this mechanism by generating Python code via the new
`evaluable.compile()` function, which produces:

```python
c0 = 1
c1 = 2
c2 = 3
def eval():
    v3 = numpy.add(c0, c1)
    v4 = numpy.add(v3, c2)
    return v4
```

In addition, subtrees that are constant are cached for a second call, providing
a slight performance improvement.

commit message:
fix basis of SimplexTopology

The implementations of the degree one std and the bubble bases for the
`SimplexTopology` incorrectly assume that the `simplices` array contains
vertex in `range(nverts)` without holes, and use this array as is as
dofs, thereby introducing zeros in the basis for every dof in
`set(range(simplices.max() + 1)) - set(simplices.flat)`. The boundary of
a `SimplexTopology`, however, simply returns a subset of the volume
`simplices` array, without renumbering.

This bug was introduced by 7e29a283, which removes `_renumber` as
preprocessor for the `simplices` parameter of
the `SimplexTopology` constructor.

To fix this problem this patch adds a `contiguous_simplices` property
and uses thses as dofs. The alternative, requiring constructing a
`SimplexTopology` with contiguous `simplices`, was rejected because this
puts a computational burden on every boundary of a `SimplexTopology`,
even if we don't create a basis.

add function._root,_tip_derivative_target

Currently gradients, normals and jacobians are computed with the local or tip

transform chains. In a series of patches the root coordinate system will be

used to compute derivative to the root coordinate system of some space, similar
to the `evaluable.LocalCoords`. In addition this patch adds
`function._tip_derivative_target` as a modern alternative to
`evaluable.LocalCoords(fromdim)`.

commit message:
Revert "replace const Arrays with Constants in optimize"

Commit f914a19b7836498f4ccd81e01fdb7b1e3a57b5ba causes constant evaluable
dependencies of some target to be evaluated and replaced with `Constant`s. This
change was assumed to be penalty free if the target is evaluated at least once.
It turns out that evaluating the constants separately during optimize and doing
one evaluation of the target is more expensive than before the commit, probably
because of duplicate work in `LoopConcatenate`s (because not combined). This
patch reverts the commit.

Fix GitHub Actions test for Numpy 1.21

The GitHub Actions workflow file should test the lowest supported version of
Numpy, 1.21, but actually installs 1.17. After installing Numpy Nutils is
installed, which lists 1.21 as minumum version of Numpy and pip upgrades Numpy
to the latest version. This patch fixes this by installing 1.21.1. To prevent
running into this issue again, this patch also installs Nutils and Numpy with
version restriction simultaneously. Pip will complain if no verion of Numpy
satisfies the restrictions.

commit message:
make Array.cast more efficient

This patch changes the way in which nested data is cast to an Array. The main
reason for the change is that the opportunistic call to _Constant was
potentially expensive, as the call to asarray (via arraydata) could lead to
expensive iteration (casting and stacking results) before concluding that the
resulting object is not actually numerical. To prevent this, we need to be able
to determine a priori whether an object can succesfully be made _Constant.
However, as valid data can take the form of deeply nested data structures, this
test is not trivial. This patch solves the problem by stacking the data in a
depth-first fashion, and conclude by either accepting the result if it is
Array, or otherwise wrapping it in a _Constant. At this stage all nested data
is taken care of by stack, and a cheap test for allowable objects remains.

where each argument has the same shape. In a follow-up commit the function
syntax will be used for derivatives: `d(u_i, x_j)` and `d(v, x_i, x_i)` as

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
replace `d(u, x_i)` with `d(u, x)_i`

The expression `d(u, x_i)` should be interpreted as the gradient of `u` w.r.t.
geometry `x`, and the resulting axis is identified with index `i`. This breaks
the assumption that functions in the namespace are treated pointwise, except
for the consumed axes. To fix this problem, this patch redefines the gradient
operator `d(...)` such that all axes of the second argument, the geometry, are
consumed and the same amount of axes, with the same shape, are generated:
`d:j(u, x_j)_i` consumes `j` and generates `i`. For brevity, this patch also
supports autoconsuming all axes of arguments parseable without indices: `d(u,
x)_i`.

Fixes #614

commit message:
remove Lowerable as Array base class

The `Lowerable` class is a protocol that describes an interface for lowering an
instance to an `evaluable.Array`. The `function.Array` implements this
interface. Currently `function.Array` explicitly derives from `Lowerable`. This
is however not a requirement and the explicit inheritance can be removed,
thereby loosing only the ability to do an `isinstance(..., Lowerable)` on
instances of `function.Array`.

In a follow-up patch the `Lowerable` interface is extended with a `spaces`
property. In `function.Array` this will be implemented using an attribute. This
is, however, incompatible with the `spaces` property as defined by the
`Lowerable` base class. To circumvent this problem, this patch removes

commit message:
add Topology.{f_index,f_coords} properties

Currently all bases compute the element index and coordinates internally given
a transform chain sequence (and the fromdims of the sequence). With tensorial
topologies the fromdims attribute will be removed, because transform chains in
a sequence may have variable fromdims, and the fromdims should be passed

`Topology`. The former is an evaluable element index, the latter the evaluable
element local coordinates. These properties are used in a follow-up patch the
arguments of the bases are changed to `index` and `coords`.

commit message:
simplify deriv of evaluable.Greater,Less,Equal

The derivatives of `evaluable.Greater`, `evaluable.Less` and `evaluable.Equal`,
subclasses of `Pointwise`, were defined as partial derivatives to its
arguments. While not wrong, `Pointwise._derivative`, in its ignorance, computes
the derivative of the arguments and multiplies this with partial derivatives
defined via `Pointwise.deriv`. Needlessly complex. This patch simply removes
the implementations of `Pointwise.deriv`, which causes `Pointwise._derivative`
to fallback to `Evaluable._derivative`. The latter immediately realises that
the result should be zero based on the dtype of the function. As a side effect
the dtype of the derivative changes from `float` to `bool`.

assemble into sorted and deduped coo directly

Currently we assemble sparse matrices as unstructured coo with repeated indices
and sort and dedup later. The downside of this approach is that we're wasting

sparse structure doesn't change.

deduped first, and the values are then inflated using the unique indices.

Constants are of compiled evaluables are stored in the compiled function's
globals under `c{index}`. When compiling `Constant(0)` and `Constant(1)` the
source codes are the same. The Nutils hash of compiled evaluables is the hash

same Nutils hash. To fix this, this patch stores constants under
`c{nutil_hash(value)}`.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
add EvaluableTransformChain

The `evaluable` module has a `TransformChain` base class with the following
problem: The to dimension is possibly undefined and the from dimension is
always undefined. This has the side effect that we need to provide both the to
and the from dimension if we want to compute the linear transformation matrix.

This patch adds a fresh `EvaluableTransformChain` to the `transform` module,
with mandatory to and from dimensions and convenience attributes for computing
linears, normals, et cetera. The old `evaluable.TransformChain` class and
subclasses will be removed in a follow-up commit. To ease the transition,

commit message:
add evaluable.IdentifierDerivativeTarget

`Array` instances define derivatives to `DerivativeTargetBase`, a subclass of
`Array`. Currently there are two kinds of targets: `Argument`, a rather
straightforward target with the identity as self-derivative, and `LocalCoords`,
which is used for derivatives to a coordinate system, described by
transformations (`nutils.transform.Transform`). Derivatives to the latter end
up in `ApplyTransforms`, at which point the derivative is defined as the linear
part of the transform of `ApplyTransforms`.

In a follow-up patch the reference coordinate system for computing gradients,
normals et cetera, will be changed from the tip or the current transform chain
(currently called the local coordinate system) to the root.

Derivatives to the root require a virtual derivative target. This patch adds a
`IdentifierDerivativeTarget`, which is similar to `LocalCoords`, but generic.

commit message:
fix incorrect usage _WithoutPoints

The `function._WithoutPoints` class is a wrapper that prevents adding points
axes to the lowered `evaluable.Array`. This is mostly useful for evaluables
that accept only scalar indices, such as `evaluable.Elemwise`. It was not
intended to be used to wrap `function.Array` instances that are publicly
exposed, like `function.Array.shape` or `function.transforms_index`, as this
breaks using the index in expressions that do require a points axis:

    topo, geom = mesh.rectilinear([2])
    altgeom = function.rootcoords(1) + topo.f_index

The `rootcoords` can only be lowered with points axis, but `topo.f_index`,
wrapped in `function._WithoutPoints`, always lowers to an array without points
axis.

This commit removes incorrect usage of `function.Array._withoutpoints` and
prevents further mistakes by not subclassing `function.Array`.

commit message:
remove shape[:-1] from LoopConcat constructor args

The shape of `LoopConcatenate` is used in the loop initialization to allocate
the output array. The length of the concatenation axis is the result of
concatenating and summing (`_SizesToOffset`) the lengths of the same axis of
the concatenation value. Under certain conditions the concatenation length
can be simplified. For this to work, the concatenation length must be a
constructor argument of `LoopConcatenate`, otherwise the length is not picked
up by `deep_replace_property`.

For the same reason the entire shape of `LoopConcatenate` was passed as
constructor argument. Since the shape of an array is very likely already
optimized --- the same is true for `LoopConcatenate.shape`! --- this patch
removes the shape from the constructor of `LoopConcatenate`, except for the
concatenation axis.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
fix importing dynamic treelog attributes

In Python 3.7 treelog has dynamic module functions pointing to the current log
instance.  For example `treelog.info` resolves to `treelog.current.info`, where
`treelog.current` is obtained when `info` is obtained from `treelog`.  In the
current code we import `info` and others from `treelog` in `nutils.log`,

    from treelog import info

which translates to

    import treelog
    info = treelog.current.info

If `treelog.current` is changed after importing `treelog`, this change is not
reflected by the local `info`.

This patch fixes the issue by resolving the attributes dynamically with the
`__getattr__` module function.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
fix simplification product of LoopSums

Currently the product of two `LoopSum`s with the same index
incorrectly simplifies to a single `LoopSum` of products. Example:

    >>> from nutils import evaluable
    >>> i = evaluable.loop_index('i', 4)
    >>> f = evaluable.loop_sum(evaluable.Guard(i), i)
    >>> g = evaluable.loop_sum(evaluable.Guard(i + evaluable.constant(1)), i)
    >>> print((f * g).simplified.asciitree())
    SUBGRAPHS
    A
    : B = Loop
    NODES
    %B0 = LoopSum
    : func = %B1 = Multiply; i:; [-inf,inf]
      : %B2 = Multiply; i:; [-inf,inf]
      | : %B3 = Guard; i:; [-inf,inf]
      | | : %B4 = Add; i:; [1,4]
      | |   : %B5 = LoopIndex
      | |   | : length = 4
      | |   : 1
      | : %B6 = Guard; i:; [-inf,inf]
      |   : %B5
      : 4

This patch fixes the problem by preventing the simplification
`LoopSum(f, i) * g -> LoopSum(f * g, i)` if `g` contains `i`.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
add spaces to Sample

Currently the `ProductTopology` relies on the bifurcate family of classes and
functions to join and separate transform chains originating from parent
topologies. This family will be replaced by the concept of spaces.

A 'space' is a Euclidean space of a certain dimension. It is identified by a
name (`str`). Every `Topology` and `Sample` has an ordered list of unique
spaces. Every element in the topology or sample is identified by a tuple of
transform chains, one for each space. The tuples of transform chains are not
necessarily maintained in a `Transforms` sequence, in part because these
sequences only cover single transform chains. `function.Array` instances can be
defined on a subset (including all or none) of spaces of a topology or sample.
Functions are assumed to be constant in spaces other than the spaces on which
they are defined, hence functions can be evaluated on a superset of spaces.

This patch adds spaces to `Sample`. In follow-up patches the spaces will be
used to instantiate `function.Array` objects and to reimplement product
samples.

commit message:
add parallel.Manager, subset of multiproc.Manager

With `parallel.fork` data cannot be shared between processes using shared
memory, except for arrays. `multiprocessing.Manager` supports sharing data via
pipes or sockets using pickle as serialization. This patch adds a minimal subset of

parallel mode is disabled, a fake manager is returned which creates regular
lists and dicts, eliminating overhead of serialization, transfering and
deserialization.

commit message:
fix derivative of evaluable.Cast

The current implementation of `Cast._derivative` casts the result of the
derivative of its argument to the desired dtype. This only works if the dtype
of the derivative is the same as that of the argument. For `FloatToComplex`
this always works, because the derivative can only be `float`. For `IntToFloat`
the derivative of its argument is always zero, but the dtype could be `int` or
`float` (which happens when you take the derivative of `Greater`). This patch
works around the problem by implementing `_derivative` for `IntToFloat` and
`FloatToComplex` separately.

commit message:
fix weights of Sample.zip (#799)

Let sample `Z` be the zip of two samples `X` and `Y`. It is guaranteed
that the order in which `Z` traverses the elements of `X` is monotonic.
Not strict monotonic, however: if the points `p` of some element `i` of
`X` are divided over `n >= 2` elements of `Y`, then element `i` is
evaluated `n` times, each with a different subset `s_j` of points `p`
and weights `w`. If the subsets `(s_j)_j` are consecutive slices,
`max(s_j) < min(s_{j+1})`, then everything works fine. If not, for the
`j`-th evaluation of element `i` points `p[s_j]` is used together with
weights `w[t_j]` instead of `w[s_j]`, where `(t_j)_j` is a sequence of
consecutive slices such that the sizes of the subsets `s_j` and `t_j`
are equal. This patch fixes this problem and adds a test for this
situation.

Fixes #791

Commit f914a19b7836498f4ccd81e01fdb7b1e3a57b5ba causes constant evaluable
dependencies of some target to be evaluated and replaced with `Constant`s. This
change was assumed to be penalty free if the target is evaluated at least once.

one evaluation of the target is more expensive than before the commit, probably
because of duplicate work in `LoopConcatenate`s (because not combined). This
patch reverts the commit.

If we call `function.Array.cast` with a list, the list is passed to
`function.take` with each element of the (outer) list cast to a
`function.Array`. If the list is a (possibly nested) list of numbers this is
unlikely the desired outcome. For example

    Array.cast([0, 1, 2])

is equivalent to

    stack([_Constant(0), _Constant(1), _Constant(2)])

Instead, this patch tries to cast the value to a `numpy.ndarray` first and, if
that works with numeric dtype, proceeds with a `function.Constant`.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
Support locating points on manifolds

`Topology.locate` requires the coordinate system per element to be smooth,
because it uses a Newton iteration to find the element-local coordinate such
that the given geometry evaluates to the given coordinate. This is problematic
when locating points on periodic domains and a geometry that wraps within an
element. Under certain circumstances we can get around this problem by treating
the domain as a manifold, e.g. a periodic line can be treated as a 1D circle in
2D space, and locating points on the manifold. This patch supports locating
points on manifolds by using a least squares solver for the Newton iteration if
necessary.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
fix simplification product of LoopSums (#816)

Currently the product of two `LoopSum`s with the same index incorrectly
simplifies to a single `LoopSum` of products. Example:

    >>> from nutils import evaluable
    >>> i = evaluable.loop_index('i', 4)
    >>> f = evaluable.loop_sum(evaluable.Guard(i), i)
    >>> g = evaluable.loop_sum(evaluable.Guard(i + evaluable.constant(1)), i)
    >>> print((f * g).simplified.asciitree())
    SUBGRAPHS
    A
    : B = Loop
    NODES
    %B0 = LoopSum
    : func = %B1 = Multiply; i:; [-inf,inf]
      : %B2 = Multiply; i:; [-inf,inf]
      | : %B3 = Guard; i:; [-inf,inf]
      | | : %B4 = Add; i:; [1,4]
      | |   : %B5 = LoopIndex
      | |   | : length = 4
      | |   : 1
      | : %B6 = Guard; i:; [-inf,inf]
      |   : %B5
      : 4

This patch fixes the problem by preventing the simplification
`LoopSum(f, i) * g -> LoopSum(f * g, i)` if `g` contains `i`.

The most recent version of MKL on PyPI ships only `libmkl_rt.so.1`, not
`libmkl_rt.so`. In Nutils we load the latter. This causes two problems: in
Github Actions we cannot find the location of the library directory where MKL

defines the output dtype for given input dtypes. This replaces the constructor

current transform chain, or we add the to dimension as an attribute to the
transforms sequence. This patch does the latter.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
replace x - (x // y) * y with x % y in divmod

`evaluable.divmod(x, y)` returns `x - (x // y) * y` as remainder. There are
three issues with this:

*   When calling `evaluable.div`, `evaluable.mod` *and* `evaluable.divmod`
    we're doing extra work. This can be solved by changing the implementation
    of `evaluable.mod`, but:

*   It appears to be cheaper to compute the modulo using `numpy.mod` on x86
    since the remainder is a byproduct of the
    [div](https://www.felixcloutier.com/x86/div) instruction.

*   `evaluable.Mod` (note the capital) has an implementation for the integer
    bounds and the remainder of `evaluable.divmod` has not.

This patch changes the implementation of the remainder of `evaluable.divmod` to
`evaluable.Mod`.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
fix gradient of function.Custom

The class `function.Custom` lowers to a class that implements
`evaluable.Array.derivative` in terms of partial derivatives of the loweree:
for all arguments that are instances of `evaluable.Array` with dtype `float` or
`complex` the `function.Custom.partial_derivative` method is called and the
result is dotted with the derivative of the argument to the derivative target.

To increase the performance of the construction of the derivative, arguments
that do not depend on the derivative target are skipped. The dependency test,
however, incorrectly uses the `Evaluable.dependencies` attribute, which does
not contain virtual derivative targets, in particular the root coordinates
(`function._root_derivative_target`). The effect of this bug is that
derivatives of lowered `function.Custom` objects to a virtual derivative target
become zero.

This patch fixes this problem by testing for existence of a derivative target
using the `Evaluable.arguments` attribute and adds a unittest.

commit message:
repl ArrayFromTuple(_lower, _upper) w tuple attr

Computing the integer bounds can be expensive. For example, a scalar array that
does not depend on arguments will be simplified and evaluated, regardless how
expensive this evaluation is and disregarding the `_intbounds_impl`.

Currently the `ArrayFromTuple` class takes integer bounds as arguments. When
combining loops, the integer bounds for the loops are evaluated, the loops are
combined and the evaluated integer bounds are passed to `ArrayFromTuple`, even
if we are not using the bounds.

To prevent evaluating the bounds, this patch introduces the `_intbounds_tuple`
property for `Evaluable`s that return tuples and replaces the integer bounds
argument from `ArrayFromTuple` with a `_intbounds_impl` that queries the
`_intbounds_tuple`.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
drop assert from _array_bases

`types.frozenarray(x, copy=False)` tries to make `x` and all of its bases
read-only. Bases are typically instances of `numpy.ndarray`, `types.arraydata`,
or `None` if there is no base. `types.frozenarray` asserts that all bases are
of these three types to make sure that we don't miss an opportunity to make a
base read-only.

In a follow-up commit the code for manipulating polynomials, `numeric.poly_*`,
will be replaced by an external module written in Rust. The arrays returned by
this module have a base of type `PySliceContainer` (provided by crate
[numpy](https://crates.io/crates/numpy)). To support making these arrays frozen
as well, this patch drops the assertion at the end of `_array_bases`, thereby
allowing all kinds of array bases.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
disallow truncation in types.arraydata

If `types.arraydata` is passed a `numpy.array` with dtype `numpy.int64` and the
platform default int type is 32 bit, then `types.arraydata` truncates the array
to `numpy.int32` without warning. This behavior is inherited from

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
Fix hash of compiled functions (#911)

The hash of compiled functions is based solely on the source code. Constants
are currently added to globals of the compiled function under `c{index}`, hence
constants are not included in the hash. Furthermore, parameters of evaluables
using `evalf` via the `e{index}` instance, also added to the globals, are also
not represented in the source code. As a consequence, two compiled functions
with different constants or parameters of certain evaluables may have the same
hash. This PR fixes the problem by storing constants under `c{hash(constant)}`
and disallowing using `e{index}.evalf`.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
add evaluable._make_loop_ids_unique

Working with `evaluable.Loop`s can be difficult if loop ids are reused in
different loops. Consider for example the following tree:

    A: LoopSum i
      B: Add
        C: LoopSum i
          D#C: _LoopIndex i
        D#A

Both loops A and C use the same id i. Consequently it is impossible to relate
D#A (the hash suffix is added for clarifation) to A and D#C to C other than by
inspecting the tree between the loop and the index: some index I belongs to
loop L if there is no other loop in between that uses the same id.

To make life easier, this patch adds `evaluable._make_loop_ids_unique`, which
replaces all loop ids of target funcs with unique loop ids if there are
duplicate ids.

commit message:
ensure Array.shape is a simplified Array or an int

This fixes the following snippet.

    from nutils import mesh, function

    domain, geom = mesh.rectilinear([[-1, 0, 1]]*2)
    domain = domain.trim(function.norm2(geom)-.5, maxrefine=0)
    function.chain([domain.basis('spline', degree=2), [1.]])

    # initialize namespace
    ns = function.Namespace()
    ns.xybasis = function.zeros([16])
    ns.phi = 'xybasis_n ?lhs_n'

The length of the first axis of `ns.xybasis` was a `numpy.int64`.  This is
unfortunately `==` to `(16,)` or `nutils.expression._Length(16)`, which
identifies the index `'n'` of `'lhs_n'`, and the unknown length is therefore
removed from the list of unknown lengths.  Hence the error

    nutils.expression.ExpressionSyntaxError: Length of axis cannot be determined from the expression.
    xybasis_n ?lhs_n
                    ^

argument if the power is a positive integer constant. Avoiding potentially
expensive evaluations, the latter is tested by an instance check. However, this
approach misses constants that are wrapped in a cast operation such as
IntToFloat. The current patch strips the power argument of casts before
proceding with the constness test.

commit message:
fix LoopSum.asarray assertion

In `LoopSum.asarray` the axes that are invariant to the loop index are shuffled

commit message:
add types.hashable_function

Plain functions are not Nutils hashable, because there is no reliable
information to generate a hash from: the name of the function cannot be used
because the behavior might be non-deterministic or can simply be changed
between different runs, and the bytecode only describes a single function, not
the functions that are being called or variables that are being accessed from
outer scopes, if any. I hear you say: 'but the dependent functions can be
distilled from the bytecode,' and: 'the closure variables are stored in the
function object.' Well, I wish you good luck with implementing a solid hash in
a Tuesday evening. This leaves us with the possibility to explicitly add a
Nutils hash to functions that need one. This commit introduces the decorator
`types.hashable_function` for this purpose.

commit message:
Reimpl function.opposite() using ~-prefixed spaces

Currently the `LowerArgs` contain a tuple of transforms sequences for each
space. Only the first item of this tuple is used in general.
`function.opposite()` reverses this tuple and passes the reversed `LowerArgs`
to its argument.

This patch reimplements `function.opposite()`. Instead of passing tuples of
transforms sequences to `LowerArgs`, the opposite transforms sequence must be
provided under `~{space}`. `function.opposite()` then swaps the ~-prefixed
space with the unprefixed space and continues lowering. Besides ditching the
tuple, this has the added benefit of allowing the coordinates and index to
change as well, which enables creating an interface using `Sample.zip`.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
fix weights of Sample.zip

Let sample `Z` be the zip of two samples `X` and `Y`. It is guaranteed
that the order in which `Z` traverses the elements of `X` is monotonic.
Not strict monotonic, however: if the points `p` of some element `i` of
`X` are divided over `n >= 2` elements of `Y`, then element `i` is
evaluated `n` times, each with a different subset `s_j` of points `p`
and weights `w`. If the subsets `(s_j)_j` are consecutive slices,
`max(s_j) < min(s_{j+1})`, then everything works fine. If not, for the
`j`-th evaluation of element `i` points `p[s_j]` is used together with
weights `w[t_j]` instead of `w[s_j]`, where `(t_j)_j` is a sequence of
consecutive slices such that the sizes of the subsets `s_j` and `t_j`
are equal. This patch fixes this problem and adds a test for this
situation.

Fixes #791

fix creating a C^0 basis on a multipatch topology

produces the following sequence of pointers:

    [1, 3] -> [0, 1, 0, 1]

patchwise dofmaps with the recently introduced `_util.merge_index_map()`.

commit message:
impl Ravel._inflations

Because `Ravel` has a higher priority than `Inflate`, it seems unnecessary to
implement `Ravel._inflations`. However, if the `Ravel` is blocked by some other
array, for instance a `LoopConcatenate`, then inflated axes cannot move down
the function tree and we miss potential simplifications. This patch implements
`Ravel._inflations` to make this kind of simplifications possible.

In addition this patch defines `Ravel._inflations` for the raveled axis if one
or both of the axes to be raveled is inflated. This makes it possible to
simplify `Take(Ravel(Inflate(...)))` to `Inflate(Take(...))`. The former arises
from slicing a basis on a product topology, which is a raveled outer product of
bases.

commit message:
fix propagation of AttrError in evaluable.asarray

`evaluable.asarray(arg)` converts its `arg` to an `evaluable.Array` by first
trying `arg.as_evaluable_array` and if this is absent calling
`numpy.array(arg)` (via `Constant`). The attribute `arg.as_evaluable_array` is

attribute is a property that somewhere down the road raises `AttributeError`,

patch fixes this problem by testing the existence of `as_evaluable_array` on
the class using `hasattr`.

concatenation of sparse terms. The swap is 1. not necessary because there is no
sparsity to be preserved, and 2. not desired, since the inflations that make up
the concatenation are not a sparse construction, so nothing is gained by
pushing the take up the tree.

by 70% (a factor 3.4) with respecto to master, and memory use by 30%.

commit message:
disallow repl f.Argument with f.Array with coords

Currently replacements are applied before derivative during lowering of
`function.Array` to `evaluable.Array`, which leads to wrong evaluables:

    a = function.Argument(a, ())
    b = function.Argument(b, ())
    c = function.derivative(a, a) # lowers to `evaluable.Ones(())`
    d = function.replace_arguments(c, dict(a=b)) # incorrectly lowers to `evaluable.Zeros`

A follow-up commit fixes this problem by applying the replacement using
`evaluable.replace`, which is only possible if the lowered replacement does not
have points axes. This patch disallows replacements with `function.Array`
objects that require points axes.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
remove points axis from coeffs in poly_eval

Currently `numeric.poly_eval` assumes the coefficients and the coordinates have
exactly one leading points axis. This patch prepares `numeric.poly_eval` for a
variable number of leading points axes in the future.

The most flexible extension is to force both the coefficients and the
coordinates to have the same leading axes. The coordinates gets one additional
axis of length `ndim` and the cooefficients `ndim` additional axes. This,
however, has a detrimental effect on the performance of `numeric.poly_eval` and
`numeric.poly_grad` when the leading axes are not allowed to be singleton.

In practice, we don't need this flexibility — coefficients never vary per point
— and it is sufficient to treat the leading axes of coordinates and
coefficients similar to an outer product: the first `coords.ndim-1` axes of the
result of `numeric.poly_eval` originate from `coords` and the next
`coeffs.ndim-coords.shape[-1]` axes originate from `coeffs`. This patch
implements this approach.

commit message:
add EvaluableTransformChain

The `evaluable` module has a `TransformChain` base class with the following
problem: The to dimension is possibly undefined and the from dimension is
always undefined. This has the side effect that we need to provide both the to
and the from dimension if we want to compute the linear transformation matrix.

This patch adds a fresh `EvaluableTransformChain` to the `transform` module,
with mandatory to and from dimensions and convenience attributes for computing
linears, normals, et cetera. The old `evaluable.TransformChain` class and
subclasses will be removed in a follow-up commit. To ease the transition,
several functions in the `evaluable` modules are adapted such that they work
with both the old and the new evaluable transform chains.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
impl Ravel._inflations

Because `Ravel` has a higher priority than `Inflate`, it seems unnecessary to
implement `Ravel._inflations`. However, if the `Ravel` is blocked by some other
array, for instance a `LoopConcatenate`, then inflated axes cannot move down
the function tree and we miss potential simplifications. This patch implements
`Ravel._inflations` to make this kind of simplifications possible.

In addition this patch defines `Ravel._inflations` for the raveled axis if one
or both of the axes to be raveled is inflated. This makes it possible to
simplify `Take(Ravel(Inflate(...)))` to `Inflate(Take(...))`. The former arises
from slicing a basis on a product topology, which is a raveled outer product of
bases.

commit message:
fix gradient of function.Custom

The class `function.Custom` lowers to a class that implements
`evaluable.Array.derivative` in terms of partial derivatives of the loweree:
for all arguments that are instances of `evaluable.Array` with dtype `float` or
`complex` the `function.Custom.partial_derivative` method is called and the
result is dotted with the derivative of the argument to the derivative target.

To increase the performance of the construction of the derivative, arguments
that do not depend on the derivative target are skipped. The dependency test,
however, incorrectly uses the `Evaluable.dependencies` attribute, which does
not contain virtual derivative targets, in particular the root coordinates
(`function._root_derivative_target`). The effect of this bug is that
derivatives of lowered `function.Custom` objects to a virtual derivative target
become zero.

This patch fixes this problem by testing for existence of a derivative target
using the `Evaluable.arguments` attribute and adds a unittest.

commit message:
add evaluable.WithDerivative

`Array` instances define derivatives to `DerivativeTargetBase`, a subclass of
`Array`. Currently there are two kinds of targets: `Argument`, a rather
straightforward target with the identity as self-derivative, and `LocalCoords`,
which is used for derivatives to a coordinate system, described by
transformations (`nutils.transform.Transform`). Derivatives to the latter end
up in `ApplyTransforms`, at which point the derivative is defined as the linear
part of the transform of `ApplyTransforms`.

In a follow-up patch the reference coordinate system for computing gradients,
normals et cetera, will be changed from the tip or the current transform chain
(currently called the local coordinate system) to the root.

Derivatives to the root require a virtual derivative target, for which the
`IdentifierDerivativeTarget` will be used - similar to `LocalCoords`, but
generic - and a special case implementation for the derivative of some `Array`
to this target. This patch adds a generic `Array` wrapper for defining a
special case derivative for an `Array`.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
rewrite evaluable loops using Loop base class

Currently there are 2.5 implementations for evaluable loops: `LoopSum`,
`LoopConcatenate` and `LoopConcatenateCombined`. The first loop is the most
common one (before sparsification). The second appears after sparsification.
The last loop is created only during the 'optimize for numpy' stage and is a
combination of several concatenates in a single loop for performance reasons.

This patch introduces a base class for evaluable loops and rewrites `LoopSum`
and `LoopConcatenate` as implementations of the base class. The base class
requires two methods to be implemented: one for initializing the output value
and one for updating the output value for each iteration.

Due to the generic nature of the base class, the method for updating the output
value is guarded with a multiprocessing lock if the loop is evaluated in
parallel, even when this is not necessary, e.g. for `LoopConcatenate`. To
minimize the impact of locking, the lock used to increment the loop index is
reused for updating the the output value.

In addition this patch replaces `LoopConcatenateCombined` with `LoopTuple`,
which supports any combination of loop evaluables, not just `LoopConcatenate`.

verify jacobian dimension if specified

During lowering of the `function._Jacobian` the dimensions of the tip
coordinates per space are known. Since the dimension of the tip coordinates is
not used before lowering, it is allowed to omit the dimension of the tip
coordinates when calling `function.jacobian`.

In the future we may incorporate units into the `function.Array`. The unit of
the jacobian is the n-th power of the unit of the geometry, with `n` the
dimension of the tip coordinates, hence if we want to define a unit for the
jacobian, we must know this dimension.

Anticipating on the introduction of units, this patch adds a check of the tip
dimension during lowering of `function._Jacobian` if this dimension is
specified (e.g. via `function.jacobian`).

commit message:
bump minimal numpy version to 1.17

This patch bumps the minimum required Numpy version from 1.16 to 1.17, which is
the first version that enables Numpy's array function protocol by default.
While Numpy 1.16 does support this protocol, it requires the
NUMPY_EXPERIMENTAL_ARRAY_FUNCTION environment to be set, which is more effort

Additionally, this patch changes the testing matrix by lowering the Python
version for which Numpy 1.17 is tested from 3.8 to 3.6, which is the highest
version for which pypi hosts precompiled wheels.

commit message:
reimpl f.Array.argshapes using f.Array.arguments

In absence of the `function.Array.arguments` attribue, the
`function.Array.argshapes` property was implemented by lowering to a
`evaluable.Array` an collecting all `evaluable.Arguments`. This is an expensive

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
fix weights of Sample.zip

Let sample `Z` be the zip of two samples `X` and `Y`. It is guaranteed
that the order in which `Z` traverses the elements of `X` is monotonic.
Not strict monotonic, however: if the points `p` of some element `i` of
`X` are divided over `n >= 2` elements of `Y`, then element `i` is
evaluated `n` times, each with a different subset `s_j` of points `p`
and weights `w`. If the subsets `(s_j)_j` are consecutive slices,
`max(s_j) < min(s_{j+1})`, then everything works fine. If not, for the
`j`-th evaluation of element `i` points `p[s_j]` is used together with
weights `w[t_j]` instead of `w[s_j]`, where `(t_j)_j` is a sequence of
consecutive slices such that the sizes of the subsets `s_j` and `t_j`
are equal. This patch fixes this problem and adds a test for this
situation.

Fixes #791

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
fix basis of SimplexTopology

The implementations of the degree one std and the bubble bases for the
`SimplexTopology` incorrectly assume that the `simplices` array contains
vertex in `range(nverts)` without holes, and use this array as is as
dofs, thereby introducing zeros in the basis for every dof in
`set(range(simplices.max() + 1)) - set(simplices.flat)`. The boundary of
a `SimplexTopology`, however, simply returns a subset of the volume
`simplices` array, without renumbering.

This bug was introduced by 7e29a283, which removes `_renumber` as
preprocessor for the `simplices` parameter of
the `SimplexTopology` constructor.

To fix this problem this patch adds a `contiguous_simplices` property
and uses thses as dofs. The alternative, requiring constructing a
`SimplexTopology` with contiguous `simplices`, was rejected because this
puts a computational burden on every boundary of a `SimplexTopology`,
even if we don't create a basis.

commit message:
use affine root coords as geom if possible (#855)

Before 5034398d3 the geometry of a rectilinear mesh with uniform vertices was
an affine transformation of the root coordinates. In patch 5034398d3 this
special case was removed due to a pending change in the transform chains for
structured topologies: the replacement of the transformation that places an
element in the root space with an index, thereby giving every element unit
square root coordinates.

The effect of this change is a suboptimal gradient of the geometry to the root
coordinates. Since the geometry is now always the inner product of a linear
basis with vertices, the gradient of the geometry does not simplify to a
constant if the vertices are evenly spaced.

This PR restores the special cased geometry for rectilinear meshes defined
by numbers of elements by creating a reference geometry out of the (unit
square) root coordinates and the element index.

author: Gertjan van Zwieten <gertjanvanzwieten@evalf.nl>
commit message:
add nutils_hash support for mutable objects

This patch adds support for mutable data. The reasons for this are threefold: 1.
the immutability was already not guaranteed by all suppored objects, namely
dataclasses and objects that define __getnewarg__, 2. dropping the immutability
requirement opens up the possibility to extend support to mutable built-in
types, and 3. the immutability requirement is not important in practice.

Mutable data was formerly explicitly excluded as a security safeguard, similar
to how Python's built-in hash function is not defined te prevent mutable
objects from being used in hash maps. The nutils hash, however, is used mainly
in on-disk caching scenarios, where it serves to fingerprint the input data
only at the moment of a function call. While this leaves the concern that the
method might modify the argument in-place (thus causing a change when a cached
return value causes the function call to be skipped entirely) these are issues
that can be dealt with at the caching level, either by adding immutibility
tests where relevant or by clear agreements that cached functions should be
clear of side effects.

commit message:
use name_of_main as fallback scriptname

This patch changes the default scriptname from argv[0] to name_of_main. The
reason for this is that argv[0] fails in scenarios such as python -m, python -m
pdb, and other alternative invocations, while name_of_main appears to be fairly
robust.

Instead of changing the default to name_of_main directly, the function default
is set to an empty string, because name_of_main is not reliable during module
initialization. The empty string is substituted by name_of_main in the function
body. Consequently, this changes the meaning of the empty scriptname from the
recently introduced behaviour (omit the script subdirectory) back to the
original behaviour (always make a script subdirectory).

when adding the path to `mkl_rt.?.dll` or `libmkl_rt.?.dylib` to `PATH` or

fails, an execption will be raised. If the user provides a path to a different
library, the behavior is undefined.

commit message:
add evaluable.WithDerivative

`Array` instances define derivatives to `DerivativeTargetBase`, a subclass of
`Array`. Currently there are two kinds of targets: `Argument`, a rather
straightforward target with the identity as self-derivative, and `LocalCoords`,
which is used for derivatives to a coordinate system, described by
transformations (`nutils.transform.Transform`). Derivatives to the latter end
up in `ApplyTransforms`, at which point the derivative is defined as the linear
part of the transform of `ApplyTransforms`.

In a follow-up patch the reference coordinate system for computing gradients,
normals et cetera, will be changed from the tip or the current transform chain
(currently called the local coordinate system) to the root.

Derivatives to the root require a virtual derivative target, for which the
`IdentifierDerivativeTarget` will be used - similar to `LocalCoords`, but
generic - and a special case implementation for the derivative of some `Array`
to this target. This patch adds a generic `Array` wrapper for defining a
special case derivative for an `Array`.

author: Gertjan van Zwieten <gertjanvanzwieten@evalf.nl>
commit message:
Add System.construct/deconstruct, add assemble arg

This patch adds the System helper methods .construct and .deconstruct, and
removes the prepare_solution_vector method. It also adds an optional second
argument to System.assemble,

The deconstruct method takes the arguments and constraints dictionaries and
returns an argument-like dictionary and a numpy array. The former contains all
the known values, i.e. all the non-trial arguments and all the constrained
values, with unknown trial values set to nan. The latter is a 1D array
containing the initial guess of the flattened and concatenated unknowns.

The construct method is the reverse operation, constructing the arguments
dictionary from the arguments-like dictionary and a solution vector.

When the System.assemble method is provided a second argument, the first is
assumed to be argument-like and the pair used in argument construction upon
entry. Upon return, the jacobian and residual are restricted to the free dofs,
which allows solvers to operate directly on the relevant solution space.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
replace evaluable.AsType with Cast

`evaluable.AsType` ensures an array has a specific dtype, applying upcasting if
necessary. If its argument already has the desired dtype, a simplification
removes the cast from the function tree.

There are two problems with this approach. Since a simplification is not
allowed to change the dtype, the simplification that removes the cast happens
if and only if its argument already has the desired dtype. In this case we
could choose to omit the cast from the start and save some steps during
simplification.

Secondly, we might benefit from moving the cast down, because integer
operations are cheaper than floating point operations and floating operations
are cheaper than complex operations. Moving `AsType` down is a bit tedious,
because the dtype of its argument can be anything. For example `Float(a) +
Float(b)` can be simplified to `Float(a + b)` only if `a` and `b` have the same
dtype.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
fix weights of Sample.zip (#792)

Let sample `Z` be the zip of two samples `X` and `Y`. It is guaranteed
that the order in which `Z` traverses the elements of `X` is monotonic.
Not strict monotonic, however: if the points `p` of some element `i` of
`X` are divided over `n >= 2` elements of `Y`, then element `i` is
evaluated `n` times, each with a different subset `s_j` of points `p`
and weights `w`. If the subsets `(s_j)_j` are consecutive slices,
`max(s_j) < min(s_{j+1})`, then everything works fine. If not, for the
`j`-th evaluation of element `i` points `p[s_j]` is used together with
weights `w[t_j]` instead of `w[s_j]`, where `(t_j)_j` is a sequence of
consecutive slices such that the sizes of the subsets `s_j` and `t_j`
are equal. This patch fixes this problem and adds a test for this
situation.

Fixes: #791

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
add spaces to Sample

Currently the `ProductTopology` relies on the bifurcate family of classes and
functions to join and separate transform chains originating from parent
topologies. This family will be replaced by the concept of spaces.

A 'space' is a Euclidean space of a certain dimension. It is identified by a
name (`str`). Every `Topology` and `Sample` has an ordered list of unique
spaces. Every element in the topology or sample is identified by a tuple of
transform chains, one for each space. The tuples of transform chains are not
necessarily maintained in a `Transforms` sequence, in part because these
sequences only cover single transform chains. `function.Array` instances can be
defined on a subset (including all or none) of spaces of a topology or sample.
Functions are assumed to be constant in spaces other than the spaces on which
they are defined, hence functions can be evaluated on a superset of spaces.

This patch adds spaces to `Sample`. In follow-up patches the spaces will be
used to instantiate `function.Array` objects and to reimplement product
samples.

commit message:
add evaluable._make_loop_ids_unique

Working with `evaluable.Loop`s can be difficult if loop ids are reused in
different loops. Consider for example the following tree:

    A: LoopSum i
      B: Add
        C: LoopSum i
          D#C: _LoopIndex i
        D#A

Both loops A and C use the same id i. Consequently it is impossible to relate
D#A (the hash suffix is added for clarifation) to A and D#C to C other than by
inspecting the tree between the loop and the index: some index I belongs to
loop L if there is no other loop in between that uses the same id.

To make life easier, this patch adds `evaluable._make_loop_ids_unique`, which
replaces all loop ids of target funcs with unique loop ids if there are
duplicate ids.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
add spaces to Topology

Currently the `ProductTopology` relies on the bifurcate family of classes and
functions to join and separate transform chains originating from parent
topologies. This family will be replaced by the concept of spaces.

A 'space' is a Euclidean space of a certain dimension. It is identified by a
name (`str`). Every `Topology` and `Sample` has an ordered list of unique
spaces. Every element in the topology or sample is identified by a tuple of
transform chains, one for each space. The tuples of transform chains are not
necessarily maintained in a `Transforms` sequence, in part because these
sequences only cover single transform chains. `function.Array` instances can be
defined on a subset (including all or none) of spaces of a topology or sample.
Functions are assumed to be constant in spaces other than the spaces on which
they are defined, hence functions can be evaluated on a superset of spaces.

This patch adds spaces to `Topology`. In follow-up patches the spaces will be
used to instantiate `Sample` and `function.Array` objects and to reimplement
product topologies.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
rewrite evaluable loops using Loop base class

Currently there are 2.5 implementations for evaluable loops: `LoopSum`,
`LoopConcatenate` and `LoopConcatenateCombined`. The first loop is the most
common one (before sparsification). The second appears after sparsification.
The last loop is created only during the 'optimize for numpy' stage and is a
combination of several concatenates in a single loop for performance reasons.

This patch introduces a base class for evaluable loops and rewrites `LoopSum`
and `LoopConcatenate` as implementations of the base class. The base class
requires two methods to be implemented: one for initializing the output value
and one for updating the output value for each iteration.

Due to the generic nature of the base class, the method for updating the output
value is guarded with a multiprocessing lock if the loop is evaluated in
parallel, even when this is not necessary, e.g. for `LoopConcatenate`. To
minimize the impact of locking, the lock used to increment the loop index is
reused for updating the the output value.

In addition this patch replaces `LoopConcatenateCombined` with `_LoopTuple`,
which supports any combination of loop evaluables, not just `LoopConcatenate`.

The derivatives of `evaluable.Greater`, `evaluable.Less` and `evaluable.Equal`,
subclasses of `Pointwise`, were defined as partial derivatives to its
arguments. While not wrong, `Pointwise._derivative`, in its ignorance, computes
the derivative of the arguments and multiplies this with partial derivatives
defined via `Pointwise.deriv`. Needlessly complex. This patch simply removes
the implementations of `Pointwise.deriv`, which causes `Pointwise._derivative`
to fallback to `Evaluable._derivative`. The latter immediately realises that
the result should be zero based on the dtype of the function. As a side effect
the dtype of the derivative changes from `float` to `bool`.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
add spaces to Topology

Currently the `ProductTopology` relies on the bifurcate family of classes and
functions to join and separate transform chains originating from parent
topologies. This family will be replaced by the concept of spaces.

A 'space' is a Euclidean space of a certain dimension. It is identified by a
name (`str`). Every `Topology` and `Sample` has an ordered list of unique
spaces. Every element in the topology or sample is identified by a tuple of
transform chains, one for each space. The tuples of transform chains are not
necessarily maintained in a `Transforms` sequence, in part because these
sequences only cover single transform chains. `function.Array` instances can be
defined on a subset (including all or none) of spaces of a topology or sample.
Functions are assumed to be constant in spaces other than the spaces on which
they are defined, hence functions can be evaluated on a superset of spaces.

This patch adds spaces to `Topology`. In follow-up patches the spaces will be
used to instantiate `Sample` and `function.Array` objects and to reimplement
product topologies.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
Fix graph of evaluables with nested loops

When building a graph of `Evaluable`s, all `Evaluable`s that are to be
evaluated in the same loop are grouped in a subgraph. The sifting logic,
however, contains a flaw. If there are two nested loops, say outer loop `a`
with index `i` and inner loop `b` with index `j`, and some evaluable `d`
depends on index `j` only,

    a = LoopSum, index i
        b = LoopSum, index j
            c = Add
                i
                d = Mul
                    j
                    2

then `d` will be incorrectly positioned outside of the subgraph of `a`. This
descision is made by `Loop._node`, which walks its descendents until an
`Evaluable` without its own loop index is found and draws those outside of the
loop. This patch fixes the bug by including all indices of *nested* loops in
the inside-outside descision making process. In the above example, when loop
`a` encounters loop `b`, the index `j` is added to the list of inside indices
for the descendents of `b` and `d` will correctly be considered being inside.

commit message:
fix axis sample._ReorderPoints

`Sample._ReorderPoints` is applied after `Sample._ConcatenatePoints` to reorder
the points according to the indices of the sample. The latter prepends an axis
to its argument, hence the first axis of the `function.Array` is the points
axis of the sample in question. When lowering the `Sample._ConcatenatePoints`
to an `evaluable.Array`, this axis comes *after* all points axes introduced by
outer integrals and samples during lowering. The implementation of
`Sample._ReorderPoints.lower`, however, incorrectly assumed the axis to reorder
was the first axis. This patch fixes the implementation.

commit message:
replace random seed by asymmetric mesh

This patch removes the initial noise that was added to the initial velocity
field to promote bifurcation, and replaces it by 90 degree rotation of the
finite element mesh. By turning the zeroth mesh line vertical, a vertical
asymmetry can be achieved by simply configuring an odd element count, which
should have a similar bifurcating effect.

A side effect of this patch is that the rotation parameter is changed in sign
so that positive rotation is now clockwise, which seems to be the more natural
direction to configure.

author: Gertjan van Zwieten <gertjanvanzwieten@evalf.nl>
commit message:
remove apply_annotations from solver module

This patch removes all apply_annotation decorators from the solver module, part
of a process to remove this construct from the entire nutils code base.

Since solver methods are user facing we cannot remove the apply_annotations
decorator by being stricter in what inputs are permissible, but instead we make
dedicated preprocessors for all objects that take care of the required
conversions, before handing over the converted arguments to the actual object
(prefixed with an underscore). The dedicated approach makes it possible to
absorbe the single_or_multiple decorator, as well as process legacy constructs
such as the lhs0 argument, and prefixed arguments such as solveargs.

In changes to the old situation, the preprocessor functions have their optional
arguments made keyword-only, and the lhs0 argument has been restricted to the
single-argument situation.

commit message:
fix parsing $ as eye in expressions

Due to a bad design choice in the expression tokenizer — insert an eye if we
match a variable with a name equal to one of the eye symbols — `$`-symbols were
not tokenized as eyes.  This patch changes the logic: if we match an eye symbol
and at the same position we can't match a (strict) longer variable, we insert
an eye, otherwise the variable.  The same logic is applied to normals.

Fixes #286.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
more strict arg processing in single_or_multiple

Since commit a77a7894 solvers support solving multiple residuals for multiple
targets. The `single_or_multiple` decorator pre- and post-processes the
arguments and results in case the solvers are called using the old syntax. Currently it is allowed
to pass a mixture of single- or multiple-style arguments to solvers, e.g.

    newton('target', [residual], ...)
    newton(['target'], residual, ...)

This commit makes the argument processing more strict: if the target is a
`str`, not a tuple of `str`, then all arguments with annotation `integraltuple`
must be not tuples as well. Similarly, if the target is a tuple, then all
arguments with annotation `integraltuple` must be tuples as well.

commit message:
fix derivative of evaluable.Cast

The current implementation of `Cast._derivative` casts the result of the
derivative of its argument to the desired dtype. This only works if the dtype
of the derivative is the same as that of the argument. For `FloatToComplex`
this always works, because the derivative can only be `float`. For `IntToFloat`
the derivative of its argument is always zero, but the dtype could be `int` or
`float` (which happens when you take the derivative of `Greater`). This patch
works around the problem by implementing `_derivative` for `IntToFloat` and
`FloatToComplex` separately.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
add spaces to function.Array

Currently the `ProductTopology` relies on the bifurcate family of classes and
functions to join and separate transform chains originating from parent
topologies. This family will be replaced by the concept of spaces.

A 'space' is a Euclidean space of a certain dimension. It is identified by a
name (`str`). Every `Topology` and `Sample` has an ordered list of unique
spaces. Every element in the topology or sample is identified by a tuple of
transform chains, one for each space. The tuples of transform chains are not
necessarily maintained in a `Transforms` sequence, in part because these
sequences only cover single transform chains. `function.Array` instances can be
defined on a subset (including all or none) of spaces of a topology or sample.
Functions are assumed to be constant in spaces other than the spaces on which
they are defined, hence functions can be evaluated on a superset of spaces.

This patch adds spaces to `function.Array`.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
rewrite evaluable loops using Loop base class

Currently there are 2.5 implementations for evaluable loops: `LoopSum`,
`LoopConcatenate` and `LoopConcatenateCombined`. The first loop is the most
common one (before sparsification). The second appears after sparsification.
The last loop is created only during the 'optimize for numpy' stage and is a
combination of several concatenates in a single loop for performance reasons.

This patch introduces a base class for evaluable loops and rewrites `LoopSum`
and `LoopConcatenate` as implementations of the base class. The base class
requires two methods to be implemented: one for initializing the output value
and one for updating the output value for each iteration.

Due to the generic nature of the base class, the method for updating the output
value is guarded with a multiprocessing lock if the loop is evaluated in
parallel, even when this is not necessary, e.g. for `LoopConcatenate`. To
minimize the impact of locking, the lock used to increment the loop index is
reused for updating the the output value.

In addition this patch replaces `LoopConcatenateCombined` with `LoopTuple`,
which supports any combination of loop evaluables, not just `LoopConcatenate`.

commit message:
redefine exterior normal with explicit reference

The sign of the exterior normal follows the sign of the determinant of the
rootgradient. For the rectilinear topologies this is usually fine. However, for
the simplex topology the sign typically flips from one element to another and
the only way to change this is to introduce a negative scaling in the transform
chain for selected elements. This is exactly how `mesh.unitsquare` solves this
problem.

This patch eliminates the dependency on the sign of the determinant of
transform chains. The `exterior` argument of `function.normal` must be a
reference geometry (with the same dimension as the topology). The rootgradient
is replaced by a gradient w.r.t. the reference.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
fix desparsify Product, Determinant, Sign

Since `Evaluable._desparsify` may return duplicate indices, either in a single
array or in multiple blocks, non-linear operations that preserve zeros cannot
be applied directly to the desparsified values. The implementations of
`Product`, `Determinant` and `Sign` currently produce incorrect results given
duplicate indices, as is demonstrated by the following:

    from nutils.evaluable import Product, InsertAxis, Inflate, Sparse
    import numpy
    a = Product(InsertAxis(Inflate([1,2], [0,0], 1), 2))
    assert isinstance(a._axes[0], Sparse)
    actual = a.eval()
    desired = numpy.zeros_like(actual)
    for ind, val in a._desparsify(0):
      numpy.add.at(desired, ind.eval(), val.eval())
      numpy.testing.assert_equal(desired, actual)

This commit removes the implementation of desparsify for the three affected
evaluables.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
remove Lowerable as Array base class

The `Lowerable` class is a protocol that describes an interface for lowering an
instance to an `evaluable.Array`. The `function.Array` implements this
interface. Currently `function.Array` explicitly derives from `Lowerable`. This
is however not a requirement and the explicit inheritance can be removed,
thereby loosing only the ability to do an `isinstance(..., Lowerable)` on
instances of `function.Array`.

In a follow-up patch the `Lowerable` interface is extended with a `spaces`
property. In `function.Array` this will be implemented using an attribute. This
is, however, incompatible with the `spaces` property as defined by the
`Lowerable` base class. To circumvent this problem, this patch removes
`Lowerable` as base cass from `function.Array`.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
fix creating a C^0 basis on a multipatch topology

The implementation for merging dofs when creating a C^0 basis on a
`MultipatchTopology` fails (with an assertion error) under certain conditions.
What happens is the following. Given four dofs on four patches, `[0, 1, 2, 3]`,
and the pairings `[0, 2]`, `[1, 3]`and `[0, 3]`, the current implementation
produces the following sequence of pointers:

    init      [0, 1, 2, 3]
    # pair -> pointers
    [0, 2] -> [0, 1, 0, 3]
    [1, 3] -> [0, 1, 0, 1]
    [0, 3] -> [0, 1, 0, 0] # incorrect!

This patch fixes the problem by replacing the implementation for merging
patchwise dofmaps with the recently introduced `_util.merge_index_map()`.

commit message:
include arguments in evaluable is constant test

The `WithDerivative` evaluable defines a derivative of a wrapped array
to some target. The target is not included in the
`Evaluable.dependencies`, but is included in the `Array.arguments`. The
current implementation of `Evaluable.isconstant` only looks at its
`.dependencies`, not its `.arguments`, giving a false positive if a
constant array is wrapped inside a `WithDerivative`. This patch fixes
the bug by testing for emptyness of `.arguments` in
`Evaluable.isconstant`, this in addition to the original test to be on
the safe side.

commit message:
avoid access to global namespace in __eq__ methods

In combination with weak key or value dictionaries it may happen that at
destruction objects in the global namespace are already replace by None,
causing in particular isinstance invocations to fail. The (binary) method
weakref._remove_dead_weakref performs an equality check, leading to unhandled
exception warnings if this check uses isinstance to check the type if the
counterpart. This patch avoids this by using type(self) rather than the global
variable. In addition it replaces isinstance with equality checks for speed.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
repl. LoopConcat with LoopSum Inflate in AtSample

The majority of the `Sample` objects being used in Nutils is of the kind
`_DefaultIndex`, which has a monotonic increasing set of indices. This implies
that `_DefaultIndex.eval(func)` is equivalent to concatenating `func` evaluated
for all elements. This is exactly how `AtSample`, used by `Sample.eval`, is
currently implemented: a `LoopConcatenate` of `func`. `Topology.locate` returns
a `_CustomIndex` sample that reorders the `AtSample` using a `Take`. The `Take`
of `LoopConcatenate`, however, turns out to be difficult to sparsify.

This patch replaces the `LoopConcatenate` with a `LoopSum` of `Inflate`, where
the indices of `Inflate` follow from the indices of the `Sample`, which
eliminates the `Take`. This seems needlessly complex for the `_DefaultIndex`
samples, because the indices are consecutive `Range` objects. However, after
sparsifying the `LoopSum` of the current implementation, the same
`LoopConcatenate` with `Range` indices are introduced, leading to equal or very
similar sparse function trees.

commit message:
reimpl f.Array.derivative using f.Array.arguments

Taking the derivative of a `function.Array` to an argument requires knowing the
shape of the argument. When `function.Array.derivative` is called with a `str`,
the shape will be obtained by lowering the array to an `evaluable.Array` and
looking up the argument in the `arguments` property. This is an expensive
operation and only works if all spaces of the `function.Array` are bound. This
patch reimplements `function.Array.derivative` using the new
`function.Array.arguments` attribute, which is inexpensive and is always
available.

commit message:
fix LoopSum.asarray assertion

In `LoopSum.asarray` the axes that are invariant to the loop index are shuffled
to the start to minimize the number of ravels. After the shuffle and ravels all
but the last axes are asserted to be invariant to the loop index. The check,
however, incorrectly checks for constness, which is more strict than being
invariant to the loop index. This patch fixes the assertion and removes an
`int` check, which is always false since the shapes are always of type
`evaluable.Array`.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
let evaluable.Reciprocal have dtype of argument

`evaluable.Reciprocal` was introduced as an optimization-for-numpy of
`Power(arg,-1)`. At that time `Power` had dtype `float` even when `arg` had
dtype `int`. Necessarily, `Reciprocal` had to inherit this behavior. This
behavior changed in the mean time: the dtype of `Power` is the same as the
dtypes of its arguments and negative integer powers are forbidden, hence
`Power.optimized_for_numpy` always calls `Reciprocal` with a `float` argument.

This patch replaces dtype `float` in `Reciprocal` with the dtype of the
argument of `Reciprocal`. This makes `Reciprocal` - and by extension `Power` -
suitable for complex-valued arguments.

author: Joost van Zwieten <joostvanzwieten@evalf.com>
commit message:
add expression parser v2

This patch adds a brand new expression parser that, for the time being, will
co-exists with the old expression parser. The new parser is private and will be
used in a to-be-introduced `Namespace` v2.

The new parser differs from the old parser in the following ways:

*   The comma notation for derivatives, e.g. `u_,i`, has been removed. Instead,
    derivatives should be defined using functions, e.g. `∇_i(u)`.

*   Besides the obligatory `+`, `-`, `^`, `/`, `(`, `[`, `{`, `<`, `)`, `]`,
    `}` and `>`, there are no symbols with special meaning.

*   The new parser cannot infer lengths of indices. For example, the shape of
    `δ` in `u_i u_j + δ_ij` cannot be infered. This is done to make the parser
    simpler. As a consequence `'?'+name` for creating arguments is not
    supported anymore.

*   The parser does not generate AST, but uses an implementation of the
    `ArrayOps` trait to produce a result.

commit message:
Passing down MPI communicators to ADIOS/casacore

Both the Table (and related) and the Adios2StMan classes on casacore
allow passing down an explicit communicator to perform collective
operations. We are now allowing OSKAR to accept such communicators,
defaulting to MPI_COMM_WORLD if nothing is given.

I've also renamed the adios2-specific method to be better aligned with
the original one.

commit message:
Reacting to early cuda runtime errors

In oskar_device_count the status flag was not being set when if a
problem was found during the call to cudaGetDeviceCount. That meant that
a call to oskar_device_count from oskar_interferometer_set_gpus failed
to recognize this problem, and behaved as if the call to
cudaGetDeviceCount had been successful (which wasn't, we were getting a
cudaErrorInsufficientDriver error when using cuda 10.0 in one of our
testing platforms).

The oskar_cuda_system_info program handles this gracefully though,
because the underlying oskar_cuda_device_info_scan function does check
the return code from cudaGetDeviceCount.

Signed-off-by: Rodrigo Tobar <rtobar@icrar.org>

Measurement Sets, which was not possible before. For this to work, removed
option to make time-snapshot images, as this concept isn't compatible

gridding functions are done in single precision. Minor optimisation to grid
index calculations.

- Added imager run log to FITS headers.
